Jurisdiction: Indonesia
Pillar: 7
Precedent tags: (none)

Scope: E-commerce platforms
Impact: Article 5 requires that transactional data related to e-commerce be stored in a way that allows for retrieval and auditability for a sufficient time, aligning with sector-specific obligations or general legal requirements (e.g., tax laws, consumer protection). 

Article 25 specify that Electronic commerce operators (PPMSE) must retain:
- Financial transaction data for 10 years from the date it was collected.
- Non-financial transaction data for 5 years from the date it was collected. Jurisdiction: Malaysia
Pillar: 6
Precedent tags: (none)

Scope: Financial service
Impact: In the Personal Data Protection Code of Practice for the Banking and Financial Sector (2017), the conditions for Transfer in Schedule 1 (Rights of Data Subjects), Section 1.1: Any cross-border transfer must ensure compliance with the PDPA’s principles, particularly related to the security of data, and must have written agreements with third-party data processors abroad. Transfer of Personal Data Abroad (Section 4.10)  prohibits the transfer of personal data abroad unless the recipient country ensures adequate protection under similar data protection laws or explicit consent from the data subject is obtained.

Jurisdiction: Indonesia
Pillar: 7
Precedent tags: (none)

Scope: Horizontal
Impact: Government Regulation Number 17 of 2025 on the Governance of Electronic System Operations for Child Protection

Part Two – Obligations of Electronic System Providers stipulates that every Electronic System Provider (ESP) must give due consideration to the best interests of the child and must prioritize the fulfillment of children’s rights and the protection of children in relation to the use of products, services, and features developed and/or operated by the ESP. 

Moreover, ESOs are required to meeting the obligations, including obtain consent from child users' parents or guardians, and conduct a personal data protection impact assessment.<|eot_id|><|start_header_id|>assistant<|end_header_id|>

Jurisdiction: India
Pillar: 7
Precedent tags: (none)

Scope: Stock exchange
Impact: Regulation 39(1) of IFSCA (Market Infrastructure Institutions) Regulations, 2021 and Rule 14 of the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Rules, 1957 requires that stock exchanges must keep the following books and records in an electronic retrieval form for minimum of 20 years:
(1) Minute books of the meetings of— (a) members; (b) governing body; (c) any standing committee or committees of the governing body or of the general body of members.
(2) Register of members showing their full names and addresses. Where any member of the stock exchange is a firm, full names and addresses of all partners shall be shown.
(3)Register of authorised clerks.
(4)Register of remisiers of authorised assistants.
(5)Record of security deposits.
(6)Margin deposits book.
(7)Ledgers.
(8)Journals.
(9)Cash book.
(10)Bank passbook
(11) such other records as may be specified by Authority from time to time.

Regulation 39(2) of the Regulation, every recognized clearing corporation shall maintain and preserve the following documents in electronic retrieval form (minimum period of 20 years):
(a) Minute books of the meetings of:
(i) governing board;
(ii) any committees of the governing board;
(b) Record of clearing members showing their full names, addresses and details of bank and depository accounts for settlement purposes;
(c) Transaction records;
(d) Record of security deposits;
(e) Margin deposits book;
(f) Client margin collection details;
(g) Ledgers;
(h) Journals;
(i) Cash book;
(j) Bank account statement;
(k) Such other records as may be specified by the Authority from time to time.

Additionally, regulation 57 of the Regulation, every recognized depository shall maintain the following documents in electronic retrieval form (a minimum period of 20 years):
a) records of securities dematerialised and rematerialised;
b) the names of the transferor, transferee, and the dates of transfer of securities;
c) a register and an index of beneficial owners;
d) details of the holding of the securities of beneficial owners as at the end of each day;
e) records of instructions received from and sent to participants, issuers, issuers’ agents and beneficial owners;
f) records of approval, notice, entry and cancellation of pledge or hypothecation, as the case may be;
g) details of participants;
h) details of securities declared to be eligible for dematerialisation in the depository; and
i) such other records as may be specified by the Authority from time to time.<|eot_id|><|start_header_id|>assistant<|end_header_id|>

Scope: Horizontal
Impact: India's framework of data protection consists of the DPDPA (2023) "An Act to provide for the processing of digital personal data in a manner that recognises both the right of individuals to protect their personal data and the need to process such personal data for lawful purposes and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto"/

Impact: This Notification is issued under the Cybersecurity Act to prescribe the roles and responsibilities of the Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT) for Organizations of Critical Information Infrastructure (CII) in Thailand. It stipulates that relevant government agencies or regulators of Organizations of Critical Information Infrastructure in each sector must establish CERTs for CIIs, ensuring they meet prescribed characteristics, duties, and responsibilities (Clause 3). Jurisdiction: India
Pillar: 7
Precedent tags: (none)

Scope: Banking companies and financial institutions
Impact: Module No.3 (clause 6) of the Banking Handbook:
Banks shall keep records of:
(a) the procedures which it has followed under this module including any documents that evidence the Client’s classification; and
(b) any notification sent to the Client under module, together with evidence of dispatch.
At least seven years from the date on which the business relationship with a client ended or for such period as may be required by any law, whichever is longer.

Module No.4 (clause 7) of the Banking Handbook:
An Authorised Promoter must keep a record of all Communications with clients Financial Promotion that it makes or approves.
The record must include at least the following detail:
(a) the name of the senior Employee who reviewed the Financial Promotion;
(b) the date the Financial Promotion was made or approved;
(c) if the Financial Promotion was in writing, a copy of the Financial Promotion; and
(d) if the Financial Promotion was not in writing, details of the Financial Promotion and its outcome, including a note stating if the Client requested the termination of a real time Financial Promotion.
The Authorised Promoter must keep the records for at least 7 years after the Financial Promotion is no longer made or for such period as may be required by any law, whichever is longer.

Module No.6 (clause 3) of the Banking Handbook:
The Banks should retain a copy of the client agreement for a period of seven years from the date on which the relationship with the relevant Client has ended or for such period as may be required by any law, whichever is longer.

Module No.8 (clause 9) of the Banking Handbook:
The Banks shall maintain record of inducements disclosed to the clients for a period of seven years after such inducement was disclosed.

Module No. 10 (clause 4) of the Banking Handbook:
The Banks must maintain a record of all complaints made against it. Note: the records should contain the name of the complainant, the substance of the complaint, a record of the BU’s response, and any other relevant correspondence or records, and the action taken by the IBU to resolve each complaint. A minimum period of seven years from the date of receipt of a complaint or the period mandated by any law, whichever is longer.

Module No.13 of the Banking Handbook:
An IFSC Covered Entity should ensure that all relevant books, and all transaction information and related information are kept –
(a) in the case of any relevant book, until at least five years after the last date of the expiry or termination of a contract, an agreement or a transaction to which the book relates;
(b) in the case of any transaction information or related information until at least five years after the
date of the expiry or termination of the contract, agreement or transaction to which the information relates.<|eot_id|><|start_header_id|>assistant<|end_header_id|>

Jurisdiction: China
Pillar: 6
Precedent tags: (none)

Scope: Industrial and telecommunication services
Impact: According to Article 3 of the Measures, Industrial data refers to data generated and collected during research and development, design, production, manufacturing, business management, operation and maintenance, and platform operation across various industries and fields within the industrial sector. Telecommunications data refers to data generated and collected during telecommunications business operations. Radio data refers to data generated and collected during radio business activities, including radio frequency data, station parameters, and other radio wave parameters.

Furthermore, Chapter 2 classifies data into "general", "important" and "core", and require firms to take different degrees of protection measures when collecting, processing, transferring, and disposing of data. 

In particular, Article 21 states that data processors in the industrial and information technology sector that collect and generate important data and core data within the territory of the People's Republic of China shall store such data domestically if required by laws and administrative regulations. If it is necessary to provide the data abroad, a data export security assessment shall be conducted in accordance with laws and regulations.<|eot_id|><|start_header_id|>assistant<|end_header_id|>

Scope: Horizontal
Impact: On 1 April 2022, the Data Availability and Transparency Act 2022 commenced, creating a new scheme for sharing Commonwealth Government data. Jurisdiction: Singapore
Pillar: 7
Precedent tags: (none)

Scope: Accounting records
Impact: According to Section 199, every company must retain accounting for a period of 5 years from the end of the financial year in which the transactions or operations to which those records relate are completed. This data shall be kept at the registered office of the company or other places in Singapore specified by the director. This provision is to ensure that the company will have sufficient data to enable them to properly audited and true financial statements.

Section 77 The Commission shall have the power to settle all offences under this Act for which the penalty is the imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months. (5) to hand over such computer data from a person having in possession or custody

Instead the Information Security Doctrine of the Russian Federation was adopted two years later (the Russian Federation No. 646 On Adopting the Doctrine of Information Security). Bank Indonesia Regulation No. 22/23/PBI/2020 on Payment Systems:
- Article 35(3) requires payment service providers (PJP) to process payment transactions domestically and retain transaction data for compliance and audit purposes. While the regulation does not explicitly state a minimum retention period, it is implied that data must be retained for as long as necessary to meet regulatory and operational requirements.

OJK Regulation No. 11/POJK.03/2022 on IT Implementation by Banks:
- Article 43(1) requires banks to manage data effectively to support business objectives, but it does not specify a minimum retention period.
However, Article 54(4) mandates that banks conduct internal audits of IT systems at least once a year, which implies that data must be retained for at least one year to support these audits.

Law No. 10 of 1998 on Banking
- The  Law No. 10 of 1998 on Banking does not specifically state that Banks are required to retain customer transaction data for at least 5 years after the account is closed. In the context of Law No. 8 of 2010, Reporting Parties includes, among others, banks as one of the financial service providers.
 
Law No.8/2023 on on the Implementation of Anti-Money Laundering (AML) Programs, Prevention of Terrorism Financing, and Prevention of Financing for the Proliferation of Weapons of Mass Destruction (WMD) in the Financial Services
- Article 63 para 1 regulates that Financial Service Providers (FSPs) are obligated to retain documents related to prospective customers, customers, or walk-in customers for at least 5 years after the end of the business relationship or the discovery of irregular transactions. Jurisdiction: Malaysia
Pillar: 7
Precedent tags: (none)

Scope: Income tax records
Impact: Section 82 imposes a legal duty on all businesses to maintain proper records and, where applicable, issue receipts. Every business must keep accurate and sufficient records for at least seven years from the end of the relevant income year to allow tax authorities to determine taxable income or losses. If gross takings exceed RM150,000 from goods or RM100,000 from services, the business must issue serially numbered printed receipts for each transaction and keep duplicates. Businesses that file late returns must also keep records for seven years from the filing date. 

If a sales recording machine is used, the receipt requirement may be waived, but only if the machine records all transactions accurately. The Director General may set or waive requirements for recordkeeping and receipts and may also request audited financial statements under the Companies Act 2016 if existing records are inadequate. Entries must be made within 60 days of each transaction. Records kept electronically must be readable, accessible, and convertible to written form; if manual records are later digitized, the originals must be preserved.

Moreover, All records that relate to any business in Malaysia shall be kept and retained in Malaysia. This includes records of (a) books of account recording receipts and payments or income and expenditure; (b) invoices, vouchers, receipts and such other documents as in the opinion of the Director General are necessary to verify the entries in any books of account; and (c) any other records as may be specified by the Director General under subsection (3).<|eot_id|><|start_header_id|>assistant<|end_header_id|>

Scope: Service tax records
Impact: Section 24 of the Service Tax Act 2018 (Act 807) sets out the obligations for recordkeeping by taxable persons. Every taxable person must keep complete, accurate, and up-to-date records of all transactions that affect or may affect their liability to service tax. This includes records of all taxable services provided or received (such as invoices, receipts, debit and credit notes), records of imported taxable services, and any other records as may be determined by the Director General. These records must be preserved for seven years from the most recent date to which they relate, must be kept in either the national language or English, and must be retained in Malaysia unless otherwise approved by the Director General under specific conditions.

If records are maintained in an electronically readable format, they must be stored in a way that allows for ready access and conversion into writing. If records originally kept in manual form are later converted to electronic form, the original manual versions must also be preserved. Copies of records are admissible in legal proceedings to the same extent as the originals. This section also applies to any person, other than a taxable person, who acquires imported taxable services in the course of business. Failure to comply with any of these requirements is an offence and may result in a fine of up to RM50,000, imprisonment of up to three years, or both. However, these obligations do not apply to foreign registered persons.

Note that this requirement was available under the repealed Goods and Services Tax Act 2014.<|eot_id|><|start_header_id|>assistant<|end_header_id|>

Impact: The Minister of Communication and Informatics Regulation No.20 of 2016 provides a legal framework for the protection of the use of personal data through electronic systems. Moreover, Law No. 27 establishes a general framework for the protection of personal data in Indonesia. It is closely aligned with international data privacy standards, and is largely modelled on the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation. Data controllers, data processors and relevant parties that process personal data are given a two year transition period following the enactment of Law No. 27, thus up to 17 October 2024 to conform with it. Once the transition period elapses, all such parties must comply with all the provisions of Law No. 27 and any noncompliance thereto may possibly be enforced.

Indonesia enacted the Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA) of 2022, establishing Indonesia’s first dedicated and comprehensive data protection framework, akin to international standards like the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Key features of the PDPA include:
	1.	Clear Definition of Personal Data and Comprehensive Rights for Data Subjects:
Article 6: Grants data subjects the right to correct and update their data.
Article 8: Provides the right to request the deletion or termination of processing personal data.
Article 9: Allows withdrawal of consent for data processing.
Article 11: Allows data subjects to limit or suspend the processing of their data
	2.	Cross-Border Transfer Rules: Allows data transfers abroad under strict conditions, ensuring equivalent protection.
Article 55: Governs cross-border transfers, permitting them only if the destination country has adequate protection measures or appropriate safeguards are in place
	3.	Data Processing Obligations: Imposes duties on data controllers and processors for secure and lawful data handling.
Article 35: Requires data controllers to implement organizational and technical measures to ensure data protection.
Article 39: Mandates appointment of a Data Protection Officer (DPO) for entities processing sensitive data or conducting large-scale processing.
Articles 40–42: Specify reporting obligations in case of data breaches, ensuring accountability and transparency
	4.	Enforcement and Penalties: Provides for administrative sanctions and criminal penalties for violations.
Article 67: Imposes administrative fines for non-compliance.
Articles 66–68: Stipulate criminal penalties for unauthorized access, misuse, or other breaches of personal data 

However, the PDPA is still being operationalized and will fully come into effect in October 2024, alongside sector-specific regulations (e.g., financial and health) that augment its application. (IV) providing personal information to overseas parties; and

These records must be preserved for seven years from the most recent date to which they relate, must be kept in either the national language or English, and must be retained in Malaysia unless otherwise approved by the Director General under specific conditions.

If records originally kept in manual form are later converted to electronic form, the original manual versions must also be preserved. Copies of records are admissible in legal proceedings to the same extent as the originals. This section also applies to any person, other than a taxable person, who acquires imported taxable services in the course of business. Failure to comply with any of these requirements is an offence and may result in a fine of up to RM50,000, imprisonment of up to three years, or both. - the transfer is necessary for the performance of a contract between the data subject and the data user; 
- the transfer is necessary for the conclusion or performance of a contract between the data user and a third party that is either entered into at the request of the data subject or in his interest; 
- the transfer is in the exercise of or to defend a legal right; 
- the transfer mitigates adverse actions against the data subjects; 
- reasonable precautions and all due diligence to ensure compliance to conditions of the Act were taken; or 
- the transfer was necessary for the protection the data subject’s vital interests or for the public interest as determined by the Minister.

Additionally, Section 6 – General Principle: Personal data shall not be processed unless the data subject consents to the processing, except in specific situations like fulfilling contractual obligations or complying with legal requirements. Section 9 – Security Principle: Data users must take practical steps to ensure personal data is protected against loss, misuse, modification, unauthorized access, or disclosure. This includes securing local processing and storage systems.

The Personal Data Protection (Amendment) Bill 2024 (Act A1727) amendments to the PDPA introduce stricter controls on cross-border data transfers, requiring organizations to assess the recipient country’s data protection framework to ensure that adequate protections are in place before transferring data. Scope: Income tax records
Impact: Section 82 imposes a legal duty on all businesses to maintain proper records and, where applicable, issue receipts. Every business must keep accurate and sufficient records for at least seven years from the end of the relevant income year to allow tax authorities to determine taxable income or losses. If gross takings exceed RM150,000 from goods or RM100,000 from services, the business must issue serially numbered printed receipts for each transaction and keep duplicates. Businesses that file late returns must also keep records for seven years from the filing date. 

If a sales recording machine is used, the receipt requirement may be waived, but only if the machine records all transactions accurately. The Director General may set or waive requirements for recordkeeping and receipts and may also request audited financial statements under the Companies Act 2016 if existing records are inadequate. Entries must be made within 60 days of each transaction. Records kept electronically must be readable, accessible, and convertible to written form; if manual records are later digitized, the originals must be preserved.

Moreover, All records that relate to any business in Malaysia shall be kept and retained in Malaysia. This includes records of (a) books of account recording receipts and payments or income and expenditure; (b) invoices, vouchers, receipts and such other documents as in the opinion of the Director General are necessary to verify the entries in any books of account; and (c) any other records as may be specified by the Director General under subsection (3).<|eot_id|><|start_header_id|>assistant<|end_header_id|>
